source.title: Five minutes to steal a Renoir: Why museum thefts are becoming bolder across Europe
source.summary: Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen.
source.evidence_text:
Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen.
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.
Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.
Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it.
Some recommendations are already being implemented, such as enhanced video surveillance, while other structural improvements are in the process of being developed.
Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.
And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October .
The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.
Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.
Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.
Now precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts including Chinese porcelain are increasingly targeted, according to Europol's report.
"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."
Christopher A Marinello, the boss of Art Recovery International that recovers stolen art, says only 5-10% of stolen art is ever recovered, making thefts from small museums like this week's "extra painful".
However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".
"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."
"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".
Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.
Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.
The Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA) says the recent thefts show "a repeated preference for small, portable, immediately accessible objects and for attacks designed to be completed in minutes".
These crimes threaten what many consider invaluable artefacts of historical and cultural value enjoyed by the public - although some people argue they steal "from the rich, who cares?" Brand says.
Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.
Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month , external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.
"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about."
Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.
Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.

discussion: The article says museums want to be open but also safe. What ideas do you have for how a museum can be both open for visitors and secure from thieves?
Think about a public place you visit. What makes you feel safe there? (For example, "I feel safe when I see many guards.")

They are becoming bolder.

grammar.explanation: The passive voice helps us describe actions where the focus is on the action itself or the receiver of the action, rather than who performed it. It's often used in news to report events without needing to name the specific person or group responsible. The present perfect passive, formed with 'has/have been + past participle,' describes an action that started in the past and continues or has an effect in the present, where the agent is unknown or less important.
grammar.example_quote: The audacious crime at the Louvre stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m has still not been recovered.

quiz.question: What is the main trend described in the article regarding museum thefts?
options: Museums are closing due to high security costs.
Museum thefts are becoming more frequent and daring across Europe.
Art is becoming less valuable to thieves.
option_feedback: This is not the main trend; while security costs are a challenge, the core issue is the nature of the thefts.
Correct! The article highlights how thefts are increasing in boldness and frequency.
This contradicts the article, which states high-value items are increasingly targeted.

quiz.question: According to the article, why are museums often considered vulnerable targets?
options: They have too many guards, which makes them easy to distract.
They often lack sufficient funds for modern security and are housed in old buildings that are hard to protect.
Most museums are in remote locations, making them easy to burgle unnoticed.
option_feedback: The article does not suggest museums have too many guards; rather, funding is an issue.
Correct. The article mentions financial challenges for security and the difficulty of protecting old buildings.
The article does not focus on remote locations but on general accessibility and historical building issues.

quiz.question: What does it mean for burglaries to become 'brazen'?
options: They are happening secretly and quietly.
They are done very openly and without fear of consequences.
They are only targeting very small items that are easy to hide.
option_feedback: No, 'brazen' means the opposite of secret; it suggests boldness and openness.
Exactly! 'Brazen' implies a shocking lack of concern for being caught or noticed.
While some items might be small, 'brazen' refers to the manner of the theft, not the size of the items.

quiz.question: Which word best replaces 'audacious' in the sentence 'The audacious crime at the Louvre stunned France'?
options: ordinary
daring
tiny
option_feedback: No, 'ordinary' means normal or common, which is the opposite of audacious.
That's right! 'Daring' means brave or bold, which is a good synonym for 'audacious'.
No, 'tiny' refers to size; 'audacious' refers to the nature of the act.

quiz.question: In the sentence, 'The stolen jewellery has still not been recovered,' why is the passive voice used?
options: To emphasize who stole the jewellery.
To highlight the fact that the jewellery is still missing, without needing to name the thieves.
To show the thieves' surprise at the difficulty of selling the items.
option_feedback: The passive voice often hides or de-emphasizes the doer of the action, so this is incorrect.
Correct! The focus is on the jewellery and its status, not on who performed the act of stealing or failing to recover it.
The passive voice here describes the state of the jewellery, not the feelings of the thieves.

quiz.question: How have the targets of museum thefts changed recently, according to the article?
options: Thieves are only stealing paintings now.
Thieves are focusing more on precious metals, gemstones, and culturally significant artefacts.
Thieves prefer very large, hard-to-move sculptures.
option_feedback: The article states that while paintings are still taken, other items are increasingly targeted.
Exactly! The report indicates a shift towards easily disposable items like metals and valuable artefacts.
The article suggests a preference for small, portable items, not large sculptures.

quiz.question: Why might Renoir paintings be more likely to be 'recovered' than the jewellery from the Louvre?
options: Renoir paintings are generally less valuable than the Louvre jewellery.
Renoir paintings are harder to sell on the black market and easier to identify, making them less desirable for thieves to keep.
The Renoir thieves were less experienced and dropped the paintings accidentally.
option_feedback: The article indicates the Renoir paintings were 'worth millions of euros', so value is not the main differentiator for recovery.
Correct! The article suggests that paintings are harder to sell, making them more likely to be found or abandoned.
While some paintings were dropped, the primary reason for likely recovery cited is the difficulty of selling them, not just the thieves' clumsiness.

quiz.question: What is a key strategy experts suggest for improving museum 'security'?
options: Hiring more art historians to identify stolen art.
Creating physical barriers that delay thieves to allow police more time or deter would-be offenders.
Removing all valuable items from public display to prevent theft entirely.
option_feedback: Hiring art historians is not mentioned as a primary security strategy in the article.
Yes, experts emphasize 'buying time' by making thefts difficult, noisy, and time-consuming through physical barriers.
While effective, removing all valuables is not presented as a suggested strategy to keep museums open to the public.

quiz.question: Which action would best 'deter' would-be offenders from attempting a museum theft?
options: Inviting them for a tour of the museum.
Making the theft process noisy, difficult, and very time-consuming.
Displaying only smaller, less valuable items.
option_feedback: Inviting offenders for a tour would not deter them; it might encourage them.
Correct! The article states that security is about 'buying time' and making theft so difficult it discourages attempts.
While this might reduce the value of what's stolen, it doesn't necessarily deter the attempt itself, as thieves might still target what's available.

grammar.explanation: Reported speech is used to convey what someone else said without quoting them directly. When reporting statements, a 'that'-clause is often used, sometimes optionally, to introduce the reported content. The tense of the verbs in the reported clause typically shifts to reflect the reporting time, and pronouns or time expressions may also change. This structure is common in news reporting to attribute information.
grammar.example_quote: Europol indicates that the number of reported museum theft cases across Europe began to increase approximately two years ago.

They are becoming more aggressive and targeting specific high-value items.
They are exclusively targeting smaller, less-known museums.
option_feedback: The article indicates an increase in thefts and a shift towards more forceful tactics, not a decrease.
Europol's report highlights 'a rise in more forceful tactics, and... a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones,' aligning with this option.
While smaller museums are targeted, the trend also includes high-profile incidents like the Louvre, and the core trend is about aggression and targets, not exclusivity.

Aggressive methods like using sledgehammers or explosives.

quiz.question: Which of the following sentences correctly uses reported speech to convey Brand's suggestion about physical barriers delaying thieves?
options: Brand had suggested, "Creating physical barriers will delay thieves."
Brand suggested that creating physical barriers would delay thieves.
Brand suggests, "To create physical barriers delays thieves."
option_feedback: This is direct speech, not reported speech, and uses an incorrect tense for the reporting verb in this context.

This is a mix of direct and indirect phrasing, and the tense and construction in the reported clause are awkward and grammatically incorrect for reported speech.

They often occupy old buildings and lack sufficient security funding.
Their exhibits are primarily composed of easily transportable items.

sentence_evidence: Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen.
When thieves broke into a French museum earlier this week and stole four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir, worth millions of euros, not everyone was surprised.
Just last month, the European policing agency (Europol) had warned that museum thefts across Europe were growing increasingly brazen.

And just days before the Renoir heist, internationally known art detective Arthur Brand predicted to the BBC that more high-profile burglaries were likely - particularly in the wake of the successful robbery at the Louvre in Paris last October .
The audacious crime in one of the world's most famous museums stunned France, and the stolen jewellery worth €88m (£75m) has still not been recovered, nearly a year on.

"We will see more of this," says Brand, "because if you are able to hit the Louvre, thieves all around the world are watching that, thinking, 'Wow' - and then they think, 'Don't we have a local museum with gold and silver?'".
Europol tells the BBC the number of museum theft cases reported to them across Europe began to increase about two years ago.

Its recent report says both the methods and targets of thefts are changing - with a rise in more forceful tactics, and, as in the Louvre case, a focus on high-value items such as precious metals and gemstones.

The Association for Research into Crimes against Art (ARCA) says the recent thefts show "a repeated preference for small, portable, immediately accessible objects and for attacks designed to be completed in minutes".
These crimes threaten what many consider invaluable artefacts of historical and cultural value enjoyed by the public - although some people argue they steal "from the rich, who cares?" Brand says.
Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.
Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.
Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.
Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month , external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

"Precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement, and facilitating illicit sales during the fencing process," it says. "Precious stones in jewellery, on the other hand, can be easily removed and sold further."

Experts say the trick is to create physical barriers that will delay thieves so there is time for the police to arrive, or to make any theft take so long that it would deter would-be offenders from attempting it.

"Security is about buying time", says Bulut. "The objective is not to make the theft theoretically impossible, but to make removal difficult, noisy, detectable and above all, time-consuming, because to be very honest, thefts can always happen, it's the timing that you're concerned about."
Sokka says it's critical to have integrated systems - so for example if an alarm goes off, you could shut down the facility, or lock down all high net worth paintings.
However, security measures are expensive. Mayor Caviezel, whose small French city hosts two museums and collections, says finding the money is "one of our main challenges".

Bulut, who sits on the International Committee for Museum Security board, says it's not all about expensive gadgets. It could also be training guards to spot suspicious people who may be casing a museum and ask them if they need help, which may deter them from returning.
"A museum cannot be a fortress," Hollein says. "We want to be open institutions; at the same time, we are facing new challenges and attacks against museums that will require new standards."
